title: Meaning of the chants and Sugar Boy Crawford's Iko Iko
summary: Cahn says the chants are pidgin English he can partly decipher; Sugar Boy Crawford's 1954 Iko Iko is played.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: We talked about, we talked about language in the Mardi Gras records, in the Indians' traditions. Was, did the words really have any meaning?

The words seem to have meaning, and they are, a lot of it is a sort of a pidgin English, and you listen real closely and listen and listen and listen. And you'll be able to pick out a number of phrases. But still there are a number that I've been unable to, to really pick out. You'll hear them say, here come a gang. Let me hear from the spy boy and so forth. But there's still a lot that I don't understand. Like Two Way Park Away, which is, I really don't know what it means. I think it's a derivative of get out of the way, I'm coming. You think that's... I think that's where it derives from.

We're going to listen to that a little while later. But first, this is a song that was done in 1954 by another New Orleans artist, who again I think was influenced by the Indians, James Sugarbar Crawford. And the song was called Ico Ico. Ico.
